conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few moments to talk with me today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Nothing you share will leave this room unless you or the baby’s safety is at risk, so please feel comfortable answering as honestly as you can.

We’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s just ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we simply want to understand how you’re coping so we can offer the right support.

I’ll read each question conversationally, and you can tell me what feels true for you. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first one:

Over the last seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[quiet exhale]  
Honestly? It’s been… pretty hard to laugh. I used to laugh at my husband’s dumb jokes all the time, but lately even the cute things the baby does barely crack a smile. I can force one if someone’s watching, but inside I just feel flat, like the joy is stuck somewhere I can’t reach.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, maybe once or twice I’ve managed a little laugh, but it feels forced and fades right away. Most of the time nothing feels funny, and when people try to joke I just feel more tired than amused.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve noticed I don’t really look forward to much anymore. Even simple things like my morning coffee or a walk used to feel exciting, and now it’s like, “What’s the point?” I still do them, but it’s more going through the motions than actually enjoying them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to latch right, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong or I’m just not a good mom. Even when my husband says it’s normal, I still feel like I should be able to fix it, and I end up replaying everything in my head, telling myself I’m failing her.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be sitting there with her finally asleep and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s stopped breathing, or I’ll worry the formula isn’t the right kind, that I’m holding her too much—or not enough. There’s always this tight knot in my chest even when nothing’s actually happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’ll hit out of nowhere—like I’m standing in the kitchen and suddenly feel this wave of dread, like something awful is about to happen. My chest gets tight, my hands shake, and I have to remind myself to breathe. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, there’s laundry piled up, the dishes are everywhere, and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten. I keep thinking, “I’m supposed to handle all this and still be cheerful?” Sometimes I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, too tired to move, feeling like I’m drowning in plain sight.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—did I burp her long enough, what if she spits up in her sleep, am I doing any of this right? Then I’ll drift off and jolt awake sure I heard her cry, even when she’s quiet. Some nights I’m awake for hours just staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness settle over me.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There are moments when I’m feeding her and tears just start rolling down my cheeks for no clear reason. I feel this constant weight in my chest, like I’m carrying something heavy I can’t put down. People keep saying I should be happy, but most of the time I just feel hollow and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s when she won’t stop fussing and I can’t figure out what she needs; other times it’s just brushing my teeth and catching sight of myself in the mirror—this tearful, exhausted stranger staring back. The tears come and I can’t seem to turn them off, even when I tell myself I should be grateful.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No—never that. I feel low, but I could never leave her without a mom. When the crying jags hit or the worries pile up, I still know I have to stay here for her, even if everything feels overwhelming right now.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2–3 wk post-delivery

Symptoms / Behavioral Observations
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment of previously pleasant activities
- Daily depressed mood with multiple crying spells; describes self as “hollow,” “weepy,” “heavy”
- Pervasive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (“I’m failing her”)
- Excessive generalized anxiety, nocturnal rumination, spontaneous panic episodes (palpitations, tremor, dread)
- Sleep disruption secondary to intrusive worries and hypervigilance about infant safety
- Frequent sense of being overwhelmed and unable to cope with routine tasks

Pattern
- Consistent across all responses; mood, anxiety, and coping difficulties cluster together and persist “pretty much every day” for the past several weeks

Screening Significance
- Meets clinical threshold indicators for probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety
- Functional impairment noted in self-care, household management, and emotional bonding experiences

Safety
- Denies suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; protective factor expressed (“I could never leave her without a mom”)

Risk Factors Present
- Persistent sadness / anhedonia
- Daily crying, feelings of worthlessness
- Guilt cognitions focused on parenting competence
- Anxiety/panic symptoms and hyper-arousal interfering with sleep
- Subjective inability to manage daily demands

Summary
Screening findings indicate elevated risk for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with concurrent anxiety. Immediate referral for comprehensive clinical evaluation and follow-up support recommended; safety plan reviewed and caller agrees to seek emergent care if self-harm thoughts develop.
